title: Understanding and Repairing Intercultural Misunderstandings
before: Explore how DSD staff separate what happened from what they inferred, and offer a specific repair after a misunderstanding.

turns.text: This course is Understanding and Repairing Intercultural Misunderstandings. It’s about the moments after something goes wrong, in a service meeting, in supervision, or with a community partner. The starting skill sounds simple. Saying “the person asked three questions” describes an exchange. Saying “the person refused to cooperate” adds an interpretation. A useful repair depends on keeping those two apart.

The course separates three things. The exchange is the words and actions. The effect is what those actions changed. The meaning is how people understood them. An accurate repair pays attention to all three while leaving motives open when we don’t have support for them. That last part is hard, because a motive often feels obvious in the moment.

The opening case makes it concrete. A family asks how a proposed change will affect daily support. A staff member ends the discussion and records the family as “resistant.” You’ll practice choosing how a responsible repair might begin. Before you choose, ask what the record now says, and what it might do to the next conversation with that family.

Because labels travel. Once “resistant” is in a record, others may treat it as settled fact, and that can reduce the family’s chances to ask questions later. The course asks us to look at what the records and responses actually show. It also reminds us that one apology, complaint, or thank-you can’t establish a whole pattern.

Let’s talk about intention, since that’s where many of us get stuck. You can explain what you meant while acknowledging what your response may have caused. But a repair loses meaning if the other person first has to agree that you meant well. And “Sorry if you were upset” says very little. Naming the actual action carries more substance.

Disagreement can look different, too. People may express it directly or indirectly, with more or less visible emotion, and neither tells us about character. In one practice situation, an employee says a development assignment “may be difficult to fit,” and the supervisor hears agreement. You’ll consider what would clarify the concern, without deciding how that employee’s community teaches respect.

There’s a public version as well. A community contributor’s question is described publicly as opposition, and they explain that it was about access. You’ll weigh how to address that misdescription. The course is careful about scope here. A practical repair addresses the unanswered question or inaccurate description, and it doesn’t promise an outcome you can’t decide.

And the other person’s response remains their own. They might accept an acknowledgment, question it, decline further discussion, or need more time. A repair doesn’t require forgiveness or a declaration that the relationship is restored. Some concerns also call for an established reporting or review process, and a conversation about communication style shouldn’t delay that required action.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite a familiar sentence: “Sorry if you misunderstood.” The task is to name the action, a feasible repair, and what remains unresolved. It’s a short exercise, but it shows how much a specific acknowledgment changes things. Clarifying questions help, too, like “What did my explanation miss?”

Those questions also protect privacy. A person can explain the practical issue without describing their identity, family history, or community. And community participants may differ about what a respectful acknowledgment should include and where it should happen. A culture brief can help you prepare questions, but it can’t decide the meaning of an apology for every person.

As you go through the course, think of an exchange from your own work that didn’t land the way you hoped. What did you observe, what followed, and what did you assume? You don’t need to share it with anyone. Bring it along privately, and see what a specific, feasible repair might look like.

guidance.title: Slowing down the story
guidance.text: When a conversation goes wrong, it is tempting to jump straight to why someone acted as they did. Try slowing down. First describe the exchange in words a neutral observer could confirm. Then name the effect: a question left unanswered, a record changed, an opportunity lost. Only then consider meaning, and keep more than one interpretation open until you have reason to narrow it.

guidance.title: A repair you could offer
guidance.text: Look again at the sentence you rewrote. Does it name what you did, or does it still center the other person’s reaction? Consider whether the repair you described is within your responsibility to offer. What would remain unresolved even after you offered it, and how would you leave room for the person to respond in their own way?
